title: Deferred execution traps
summary: Streaming versus buffering operators, captured variables that change, exceptions that surface late, and bugs from enumerating twice.

steps.title: Streaming and buffering
body: Most operators **stream**: they pass each item on as soon as they have it (`Where`, `Select`, `Take`, `SelectMany`, `Zip`).
Some must see **every** item before they can hand out even the first. They **buffer**:
- `OrderBy`: the smallest item could be the last one.
- `GroupBy`: a group is not complete until the end.
- `Reverse`: the last item has to come out first.
Watch this pipeline. Every item runs through the first `Select` before **anything** leaves `OrderBy`, then the sorted items stream out through the last `Select` one by one.
Why it matters: `OrderBy` on an infinite sequence never finishes, and `.OrderBy(...).First()` still reads the whole source.

steps.prompt: Each stage prints as it runs. What does this print?
steps.explain: `OrderBy` buffers, so all three `a` lines run first, even though only two items are wanted. After the sort, items stream again: `b1`, then the loop body, then `b2`. `Take(2)` stops before `b3`.

steps.title: The query reads variables late
body: A lambda does not copy the variables it uses. It **captures** them, and reads their value **when it runs**, which for a lazy query is when you enumerate.
```csharp
int minAge = 18;
var adults = people.Where(p => p.Age >= minAge);
minAge = 65;                // changes the query!
foreach (var p in adults)   // runs now, with minAge = 65
The same goes for the source: a query over a `List` sees items added **after** the query was built, because it only reads the list when enumerated.
That can be handy (one query, reused as data changes) or a nasty bug. When you want "the answer as of now", call `ToList()` right away.

steps.explain: `passed` runs at the `string.Join`, so it sees the new threshold 80 **and** the new score 85. `snapshot` ran when `ToList()` was called, with 50 and the old list, and never changes again.

steps.title: Exceptions show up late
body: Because nothing runs when a query is built, nothing can **fail** then either.
```csharp
List<int> parsed;
IEnumerable<int> numbers;
try
numbers = lines.Select(int.Parse);   // nothing parsed yet
catch (FormatException) { ... }          // never catches anything
parsed = numbers.ToList();               // throws HERE, outside the try
The exception is thrown wherever the query is **enumerated**: maybe in another method, or much later. The stack trace then points somewhere surprising.
The fix: enumerate (`ToList()`) **inside** the `try`, or handle bad items in the query itself, for example with `int.TryParse`.

steps.prompt: `"x"` is not a number. Which line throws the `FormatException`?
steps.explain: Lines 1 and 2 only build recipes. Line 3 enumerates, but `First()` stops after `"4"` and never reaches `"x"`. Line 4 has to look at every item, so it is the one that parses `"x"` and throws.

steps.title: Changing a list while a query reads it
body: A query over a `List<T>` holds an enumerator on that list. If the list changes **while** the query is being enumerated, the enumerator throws `InvalidOperationException: Collection was modified`.
```csharp
var overdue = invoices.Where(i => i.DaysLate > 30);
foreach (var inv in overdue)
invoices.Remove(inv);        // throws on the next step
The query reads `invoices` lazily, so removing from it mid-loop breaks the walk. Materialise first:
```csharp
foreach (var inv in overdue.ToList())   // a separate copy to walk over
invoices.Remove(inv);
(`invoices.RemoveAll(i => i.DaysLate > 30)` is even simpler.)

steps.title: Ticket numbers that keep changing
prompt: `Issue` gives each request a ticket number, starting at `start`. The tests call it and then look at the result **twice**: once to count, once to print. The numbers come out different each time.
Fix it so the ticket numbers are given out exactly once. Keep the `Select` that numbers them.
starter: static IEnumerable<string> Issue(List<string> requests, int start)
solution: static IEnumerable<string> Issue(List<string> requests, int start)
template: Dojo.Eq("numbered from 100, even when read again", new List<string> { "#100 printer", "#101 vpn", "#102 login" }, dojoTickets.ToList());
Dojo.Eq("still the same the third time", "#100 printer", dojoTickets.First());
hints: Each time the tests enumerate the result, the lambda runs again and `next` keeps counting up.
Run the query once, at the moment `Issue` is called.

steps.title: Filters that all look the same
prompt: `Buckets` builds one filter per remainder, then counts how many numbers fall into each: `Buckets([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7], 3)` should be `[2, 3, 2]` (remainder 0: 3 and 6; remainder 1: 1, 4 and 7; remainder 2: 2 and 5).
It returns `[0, 0, 0]`. Every lambda captured the **same** `i`, and reads it after the loop has finished, when it is `3`. Fix it so each filter keeps its own remainder.
starter: static List<int> Buckets(List<int> nums, int k)
solution: static List<int> Buckets(List<int> nums, int k)
hints: A `for` loop has **one** `i` for the whole loop. Every lambda reads that one variable.
Declare a new variable inside the loop body. Each pass gets its own copy.
`{ int r = i; filters.Add(n => n % k == r); }`. (A `foreach` over `Enumerable.Range(0, k)` also works: it makes a fresh variable each pass.)

steps.title: Parse safely, fail early
prompt: Readings arrive as text. Write `static List<int> ParseReadings(List<string> raw)`:
- trim each value; skip blank ones
- if any remaining value is not a whole number, throw `FormatException` **from inside this method** (so callers see the error at the call, not later)
Use LINQ for the work, and make sure the whole query has run before the method returns.
template: Dojo.Eq("parses and skips blanks", new List<int> { 4, 12, -3 }, ParseReadings(new List<string> { " 4", "", "12 ", "   ", "-3" }));
Dojo.Throws<FormatException>("a bad value throws during the call", () => ParseReadings(new List<string> { "1", "two", "3" }));
Dojo.Eq("nothing to parse", new List<int>(), ParseReadings(new List<string> { " " }));
hints: `Select(s => s.Trim())`, then `Where` to drop the empty ones.
`int.Parse` throws `FormatException` on bad text: that is the behaviour you want.
Return type is `List<int>`, so finish with `.ToList()`: that is what makes it run, and throw, inside the method.
